1. The animation shows a grid of historical start months. Each cell is a month when someone could have started buying, and the cell is lit if the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark cells are months where the renter was ahead. It is labeled "illustrative" and draws on FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The scenario is a "rent tag 4%", and the buyer comes out ahead in 64.2% of start months.

2. The dark band in the middle of the grid grows and settles. In frame 1, one column in the band is still being filled in. By frames 4 to 6, the band has settled at its final shape. The "rent tag 4%: buyer ahead in 64.2% of start months" caption appears in frame 4 and stays on screen. Most of the grid stays lit, with a dark stretch in the middle and a few dark cells at the left edge.

3. In this historical data, buying beat renting over a ten-year hold in about two-thirds of start months, and renting won in about one-third. The renter-ahead months are bunched together, so the result depends on when you start. It does not come out the same every time. The bottom caption says "US only · history, not a forecast," so this describes the past and does not predict the future.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually, but not always, paid off over ten years. They might also take away that timing matters and that the outcome depends on the rent assumption.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only gives the 64.2% figure, the legend and the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer. It never tells the viewer to buy or to rent.
